exercise1.prompt: Rows and Columns with Lists: Pull out a column

hiddenCases.name: scores really is a list of the three numbers
the column is taken from the table

exercise1.hint: One value per row, always at the same position. A comprehension over the rows is the shortest way to say that.

exercise2.prompt: Rows and Columns with Lists: A column, filtered

hiddenCases.name: a subject nobody takes gives an empty list
the order of the table is kept
an empty table gives an empty list
the column is filtered with a comprehension or loop

exercise2.hint: The subject is at position 2 and the name at position 0: [row[0] for row in table if row[2] == subject].

questions.prompt: A table has rows [["Ada", 8], ["Grace", 10], ["Lin", 6]]. What does table[2][0] select?
choices: "Ada": the first field in the first row
6: the second field in the third row
"Lin": the first field in the third row
questions.explain: Indexes start at zero. table[2] first selects ["Lin", 6]; [0] then selects its first field. Trace one bracket pair at a time instead of treating the two indexes as a column lookup.

questions.prompt: What is the weakness of storing rows as plain lists?
choices: You have to remember what each position means
questions.explain: row[1] tells you nothing about what it holds. Six months later, neither does the code.

questions.prompt: To collect one column you build a new list with a ___ over the rows.
questions.explain: A comprehension states the shape of the result, which is what makes a column extraction read as one idea.

questions.prompt: A column is inserted at position 1 of every row. What happens to code that reads row[1] as the score?
choices: It silently reads the new column instead
questions.explain: Nothing raises, which is the danger. The summary is computed over the wrong column and looks perfectly plausible.

questions.prompt: Match each idea to its meaning.
right: The second value in the first row
The second column collected from every row
questions.hint: Read nested indexing one bracket at a time. A comprehension repeats a selection across rows.
questions.explain: rows[0]: The first complete row. rows[0][1]: The second value in the first row. [row[1] for row in rows]: The second column collected from every row.

questions.prompt: Arrange these steps in the intended order.
questions.hint: Find the first step that does not depend on any earlier result. Then follow each dependency.
questions.explain: Extract the numeric column before summing; summing the rows themselves is a different operation.

questions.label: Predict the first line of output (without surrounding quotes).
questions.prompt:
rows = [["Ada", 8], ["Grace", 10], ["Lin", 6]]
print(rows[1][0])
scores = [row[1] for row in rows]
print(sum(scores))

First output line: ___
questions.hint: Trace each line in order and write down the current values. Stop at the first print call.
questions.explain: rows[1] is ["Grace", 10], then [0] selects Grace from that row. The comprehension selects position 1 from every row, producing [8, 10, 6]. Summing this column gives 24.
